This misalignment creates a structural singularity, maximizing injury risk while yielding zero marginal gain in competitive performance.

We define the primary objective function of early-season practice as minimizing the probability of injury, P(injury), while maximizing tactical readiness, T. The 'falling on the ball' exercise introduces a massive perturbation to P(injury) via high-friction interactions with the turf, yet yields a near-zero contribution to T. Mathematically, this drill occupies the null space of the tactical projection operator. The persistence of this practice is not driven by optimization but by path dependence—a historical inertia where low-complexity coaching inputs (bawling instructions) exploit the easiest available state transition for neophytes. In our GSI/GSE framework, we treat this as a degenerate kernel. The coach acts as a rudimentary controller applying a constant, uninformative force vector, causing the athlete's state to slide along a trajectory of maximum entropy production (abrasion, fatigue) without approaching the target manifold of game-ready skills. The 'leathern lung' signifies an analog feedback loop completely decoupled from quantitative performance metrics. By mapping this to a Bayesian inference model, we observe that the prior belief in the utility of such hardening is overwhelmingly rejected by the likelihood of injury and the posterior realization of its tactical uselessness. The system breaks down when the cumulative damage from these null-space operations exceeds the biological repair capacity of the agent, leading to a catastrophic reduction in squad availability. Thus, the sovereign primitive here is the identification and excision of operators that maximize physical cost while projecting orthogonal to strategic gain.
